reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / standard medical genetics references
clinicalPearls: Core features arise from abnormal development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches, affecting the thymus, parathyroids, and cardiac outflow tract
Conotruncal cardiac defects such as tetralogy of Fallot, interrupted aortic arch, and truncus arteriosus are common
Hypocalcaemia from parathyroid hypoplasia may present with neonatal tetany or seizures
Thymic hypoplasia causes variable T-cell immunodeficiency and susceptibility to infection
Characteristic facial features, cleft palate or velopharyngeal insufficiency, and feeding and speech difficulties are frequent
Caused by a microdeletion at chromosome 22q11.2, the most common human microdeletion syndrome
Neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions, including a raised risk of schizophrenia in adulthood, are important later concerns
Presentation is highly variable, ranging from severe neonatal illness to mild features diagnosed incidentally
reference.pathophysiology: DiGeorge syndrome is most often caused by a recurrent hemizygous microdeletion at chromosome 22q11.2, encompassing the TBX1 gene among others. TBX1 is critical for development of the pharyngeal arches and pouches, and its haploinsufficiency disrupts formation of the thymus, parathyroid glands, and cardiac outflow tract, producing immunodeficiency, hypoparathyroidism with hypocalcaemia, and conotruncal heart defects. The deletion typically arises de novo from misalignment of flanking low-copy repeats, though it can be inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Similar phenotypes rarely result from other causes such as maternal diabetes or teratogen exposure.
additionalInvestigations: Chromosomal microarray or targeted FISH for the 22q11.2 deletion
Serum calcium, phosphate, and parathyroid hormone measurement
Immunological evaluation including T-cell subsets and lymphocyte function
Palate, feeding, hearing, and developmental assessments
redFlags: Neonatal hypocalcaemia causing seizures or tetany requiring urgent correction
Severe cardiac defects presenting with cyanosis or shock in the newborn
Profound T-cell immunodeficiency needing irradiated, cytomegalovirus-safe blood products and caution with live vaccines
Later emergence of serious psychiatric illness warranting monitoring in adolescence and adulthood
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends chiefly on the severity of cardiac disease and immunodeficiency; most children with milder immune involvement do well, while those with complete thymic aplasia face life-threatening infection unless treated with thymic or immune reconstitution.
pitfalls: Overlooking hypocalcaemia as a cause of neonatal seizures
Giving non-irradiated blood or live vaccines to a severely immunodeficient infant
Assuming normal cognition and missing learning and psychiatric needs
Failing to consider the diagnosis in an isolated conotruncal cardiac lesion
management: Correct hypoparathyroid hypocalcaemia with calcium and activated vitamin D analogues such as alfacalcidol or calcitriol, treating neonatal tetany or seizures urgently
Surgical correction of conotruncal cardiac defects such as tetralogy of Fallot, interrupted aortic arch or truncus arteriosus with paediatric cardiology and cardiac surgery
Immunological management guided by T-cell studies, with thymic transplantation or haematopoietic reconstitution for complete athymia and antimicrobial prophylaxis or immunoglobulin support otherwise
Avoid live vaccines and use irradiated, cytomegalovirus-negative blood products where significant T-cell immunodeficiency exists
Repair of cleft palate or velopharyngeal insufficiency with speech, feeding and hearing therapy
Developmental, educational and psychiatric support given learning difficulty and later psychiatric risk
Genetic counselling with parental testing for the 22q11.2 microdeletion, which is usually de novo but autosomal dominant when inherited
